# Public-key cryptography and digital signatures (`public_key_cryptography`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/computing.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Computing, control & information theory (`computing`)
- Deps: needs cryptography; helped by programmable_computer, algorithm_concept, prime_numbers_number_theory
- Core idea: Two people with authenticated public information can agree on a secret over a line that everyone can hear. Diffie–Hellman lets both parties derive the same key from their private choices and public messages. RSA uses a different asymmetry: multiplying two large primes is easy, while recovering them from their product can be prohibitively costly at a suitable key size. Each person makes a pair of keys, publishes one and keeps the other. Anyone can encipher with the public key, but only the owner of the private key can decipher. A signature algorithm uses a private signing key to sign a message and a public verification key to check it. These methods reduce the need for secret couriers, but the recipient still needs an authentic public key.
- Pitfalls:
  - Assuming that sender and receiver must always share a secret beforehand; this was held to be self-evident until the 1970s
  - Keys that are too short, or primes produced by a poor random source, which can be recovered
  - Accepting a public key without checking whose it is; an attacker in the middle can substitute his own
  - Claiming it is proven unbreakable; unlike the one-time pad its safety rests on problems believed, not proven, to be hard
- History: europe: 1874 – Jevons remarks how hard it is to undo a multiplication of two primes; 1970–1974 Ellis, Cocks and Williamson at GCHQ find the idea, the prime-product scheme and the key exchange in secret (made public in 1997); americas: 1974 – Merkle's puzzles; 1976 Diffie and Hellman, New Directions in Cryptography; 1977 Rivest, Shamir and Adleman's RSA system, published 1978
- Read:
  - Whitfield Diffie & Martin E. Hellman, New Directions in Cryptography, IEEE Transactions on Information Theory 22 (1976)
  - Steven Levy, Crypto: How the Code Rebels Beat the Government (2001)
  - Simon Singh, The Code Book (1999)
